JSON: Name: gnn_aclp_pipeline Title: SEAL-based graph neural network pipeline for port-level analog circuit link prediction from incomplete netlists Short Hypothesis: Applying a SEAL subgraph-based GNN (DRNL node labeling plus native component features) to port-level circuit graphs will increase link-prediction accuracy by at least 10 percentage points relative to heuristic, latent-feature, and standard node-centric GNN baselines on curated SPICE-derived datasets under intra-dataset and cross-dataset evaluations. Related Work: Existing link-prediction approaches fall into three groups: heuristic/topological scores (e.g., common neighbors, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar) that are low-cost and interpretable but fail on sparse, heterogeneous circuit graphs; latent-feature/factorization methods that capture global structure but depend on dense interactions and strong factorization assumptions, reducing robustness on small or noisy datasets; and learning-based graph neural networks that model node/edge patterns but typically operate at component-level or require large annotated corpora and unified formats. Hypergraph or tensor-based models capture higher-order interactions but incur rapidly growing computational cost as hyperedge order increases. Prior netlist parsing efforts either assume fixed formats or use LLMs without retrieval grounding, which introduces format incompatibility and hallucination risk. In summary, current methods either lack port-level expressiveness, do not generalize across heterogeneous netlist formats, or are computationally infeasible at scale. Abstract: Analog circuit link prediction—identifying missing port-to-port connections in incomplete netlists—is critical for automated analog design workflows but is hindered by heterogeneous netlist formats, limited annotated data, and topology-sensitive requirements. We present a structured pipeline that (1) models netlists at the port level and applies the SEAL subgraph-learning framework with DRNL node labeling and native component features inside a DGCNN encoder for port-level link prediction; (2) uses Netlist Babel Fish, a retrieval-augmented-generation (RAG) LLM-backed converter grounded on a SPICE knowledge base, to unify and convert diverse netlist formats; and (3) provides a curated SpiceNetlist dataset of 775 annotated circuits and a preprocessing pipeline using PySpice validation and manual correction to ensure format consistency. The main contribution is an end-to-end, format-tolerant training and evaluation pipeline that targets port-level prediction accuracy and cross-dataset generalization. We expect the pipeline to yield significantly higher port-level prediction accuracy and robust transfer across datasets while exposing linear computational scaling that informs future optimization work. Experiments: Datasets: SpiceNetlist (775 annotated circuits, 10 component classes, avg nodes 13.78, avg edges 15.60), Image2Net (1960 graphs, 13 classes, avg nodes 26.36), Masala-CHAI (4057 graphs, 13 classes, avg nodes 15.72), AnalogGenie (use random 10% representative subset ~406 graphs). Preprocessing: run PySpice syntactic validation to filter bad SPICE files, convert SPICE↔JSON via Netlist Babel Fish with RAG+LLM, and manually correct content errors; represent graphs at port-level, stack adjacency matrices (block-diagonal) for batching. Model and training: SEAL framework with DRNL one-hot labeling concatenated with one-hot component-type features; DGCNN encoder; 2-hop enclosing subgraphs; batch_size=1; max_epochs=50; early stopping engaged after test accuracy >0.5 then stop if no improvement ≥1e-4 for 3 epochs; learning rates: 1e-6 for SpiceNetlist, 1e-6 baseline for Image2Net/Masala-CHAI and 6e-8 for proposed method on those datasets; repeat protocol: for each test graph randomly select one vertex and predict its neighbors; repeat 10 times per run and report mean±std. Evaluation protocols: intra-dataset (train/val/test split 70/10/20 and separate 5-fold cross-validation) and cross-dataset (train on one dataset, test on another, include AnalogGenie). Baselines: heuristic scores (common neighbors, Jaccard, Adamic-Adar, preferential attachment, resource allocation, Katz, PageRank, SimRank), latent-feature/factorization methods (SBM, BMF, AROPE, graph2vec, SPC), representative GNN alternatives (VGAE, GraphSAGE, GCN+LRGA), previous published baseline for circuit completion. Metrics: accuracy (port-level link presence), ROC-AUC, average inference time per graph (including subgraph extraction), peak RAM, peak VRAM, and flags for OOM/OOT; report mean±std. Ablation studies: (a) replace SEAL with node-centric GNN baselines and latent/heuristic methods to quantify SEAL gain; (b) ablate DRNL labeling and/or native component features to measure contribution of each input feature; (c) compare subgraph extraction strategies: SEAL (enclosing k-hop), ScaLed (random-walk samples), and SUREL+ (offline sampled sets) and measure trade-offs between accuracy, ROC-AUC, and inference time. Statistical testing: paired t-tests between proposed method and top baselines across runs, significance at p<0.05. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Computational scalability: SEAL's enclosing-subgraph extraction and DRNL labeling scale linearly with average edges and total edges, causing high runtime and memory (RAM/VRAM) and OOM/OOT failures on large or very dense netlists. 2) Multiple valid completions: port-level problem is inherently non-unique—there can be multiple electrically plausible completions—so accuracy metrics may penalize alternative valid solutions. 3) Dataset biases and annotation quality: SpiceNetlist and aggregated datasets may contain labelling or sampling biases (component mix, circuit types) limiting generalization to unseen circuit topologies. 4) LLM and RAG failure modes: Netlist Babel Fish may introduce incorrect conversions or hallucinated port assignments when knowledge-base retrieval is insufficient or prompts are ambiguous, producing downstream training noise. 5) Evaluation limitations: node-level accuracy and ROC-AUC do not guarantee circuit electrical correctness; predicted links may be topologically correct but electrically invalid. 6) Format and domain drift: custom or proprietary netlist variants and novel component types not covered by the knowledge base will reduce parsing and prediction performance. 7) Dependence on manual correction: preprocessing requires human verification for content errors, limiting full automation and reproducibility. 8) Dense-graph degradation: SEAL and DRNL may struggle to distinguish informative substructures in highly dense graphs, reducing predictive utility on such datasets.
